opening.headline: We explain how to handle users leaving after waiting for a long response and occasionally broken JSON parsing by forcing streaming and schema, respectively.
body: If a user sends a question and the screen stays blank until the response is completed and only shows a loading sign, the longer the response, the more likely the user will leave midway. Meanwhile, the API that extracts order information must return JSON, but sometimes explanatory sentences are added in front of the JSON or field names are changed, causing parsing to fail.

In this class, we'll look at how streaming works, taking the response in pieces, and how to enforce the output structure with a JSON schema. It also distinguishes between schema enforcement and prompting, and what the app needs to check even if a schema is used.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain streaming and JSON schema-based structured output
You can find the cause of parsing failure by distinguishing between schema enforcement and prompt instructions.

screens.title: If you wait and leave, parsing of the received JSON is broken.
screens.lead: Read the two questions below. Although they may seem like different problems, they are all related to how you receive a response.

visual.alt: A scene that juxtaposes two problems: a user waiting on a blank screen and a malformed JSON response.
labels: Blank screen until response is finished

paragraphs: This is the first problem. When a user sends a question, the screen remains blank and displays a loading indicator until the entire response is completed. Longer responses lead to longer wait times, and users leave before seeing results. Even though the model already had something to show by the time it wrote its first words.

This is the second problem. The order extraction API expects JSON, sometimes prefixed with the statement "Here are the results:". Some responses have the field name `id` instead of `order_id` or are missing required fields. The app's parser cannot read this response and throws an error.

Waiting comes from the method of receiving responses all at once, while parsing failure comes from the method of only requesting the output format. This class explores whether these two can be solved with streaming and schema forcing, respectively.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can waiting be solved with streaming and parsing failure with schema? And is there anything to be careful about when using the two solutions together?

screens.outro: First, let's recall how my app displays long responses.

screens.title: How do I display long responses on the screen?
screens.lead: Read the two methods below and think about which one your app is closer to. There is no set answer and you will not enter or submit it.

paragraphs: Method A is a method where all responses are displayed at once. It has the advantage of being simple to implement and that the completed results can be processed at once. But the longer the response, the more the user waits without seeing anything.

Method B is a method of displaying information little by little as it is created. Since the first letter is visible immediately, the perceived waiting time is reduced. However, since the response comes in fragments, code to receive the fragments is needed.

Let me add one more question here. If the response is JSON, do I have to get to the end to parse it? The JSON received in pieces has no grammar before it is completed. Check the answer to this question on the demo screen.

callout.label: think about it
callout.text: Is my app Type A or Type B? Why?

screens.outro: Let’s start by checking out how streaming actually works.

screens.title: Streaming: Receiving the response in pieces
screens.lead: Each time you select the right arrow, an event will arrive one by one. Follow Claude's flow of streaming events in order.

visual.alt: Streaming events arrive from top to bottom, increasing screen text piece by piece.
labels: When text_delta comes, add one piece at a time

steps.title: Turn on streaming
steps.body: When Claude gives the request `stream: true`, it gradually sends a response as server-sent events (SSE). Pieces arrive as they are created, without waiting for the response to be completed.

steps.title: message_start and content blocks
steps.body: First comes the `message_start` event, followed by `content_block_start`, one or more `content_block_delta`, and `content_block_stop` for each content block. `index` in each block corresponds to the `content` array position in the final message.

steps.title: Text fragment: text_delta
steps.body: The text arrives little by little as the `text_delta` event. The app simply attaches the arriving fragment to the end of the text on the screen. `ping` events may be mixed in, so ignore unknown events.

steps.title: JSON fragment: input_json_delta
steps.body: The tool call input is a partial JSON string arriving as `input_json_delta`. This fragment is not valid JSON until it is complete, so you need to parse it after `content_block_stop` at the end of the block. Here are the answers to the questions asked on the activation screen.

steps.title: Closure and Errors
steps.body: The response ends with the `message_delta` event and the final `message_stop` event. Even during streaming, error events such as `overloaded_error` may occur. You can also use the SDK's `get_final_message()` to collect the pieces and receive the final message at once.

screens.outro: Now that we've saved you some waiting with streaming, let's read the schema that enforces the format.

screens.title: JSON Schema: What Every Line Decides
screens.lead: Read the schema for order extraction. In the explanation on the right, you can see what each line determines and the symptoms when that line is missing or misaligned.

notes.note: Schema is a blueprint (JSON Schema) that lists JSON field names, types, and whether they are required. Determine that the top level is an object. In Claude, this schema must be sent as `json_schema` to `output_config.format` to enable forcing. If it is omitted, it is a plain text response, so sentences may be attached.

Set the field name and type. If your app code reads `id`, but it is written as `order_id` in the schema, the app will not find the value. Gemini guides the schema to `properties`, concrete types (integer, string, enum), and `description`.
Determine required fields. Fields not in this list may be omitted from the response, and their omission is not a schema violation.
Blocks items outside the defined fields. OpenAI strictly applies the schema by using `strict: true`, `required`, and `additionalProperties: false` together.

screens.outro: Now that we've read the schema, let's compare forcing the schema and asking for it with a prompt.

screens.title: Schema enforcement and prompt instructions
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the response to the same order extraction request changes. At the end, we also check what the schema does not guarantee.

states.label: prompt instruction
states.body: Even if you write “Answer only in JSON” to a prompt, the model can preface it with sentences like “Here are the results:” and change field names or omit required fields. Asking in sentences does not guarantee structure. OpenAI also explains that JSON mode only guarantees valid JSON and does not guarantee schema compliance. So your app should have separate code to polish or retry the response. The problem is that if you send the same request ten times, even if it comes back nine times, one incorrect response can spread to an error in the entire service.

states.label: Schema enforcement
states.body: According to Claude's documentation, schema coercion is achieved with constrained decoding, ensuring no `JSON.parse` errors and guaranteed field types and required fields. OpenAI's advantages include type safety, simpler prompts, and programmatic detection of safe rejections. However, the meaning of the value is not guaranteed. The Gemini document instructs you to verify the value in the app even if it is grammatically correct JSON. Claude has a grammar compilation delay the first time a new schema is written, and compiled grammars are cached 24 hours after the last use. So, you should be aware that the first call can be slow during development stages where you frequently change schema.

screens.outro: Now that we have completed the comparison, let's classify the causes of parsing failure by case.

screens.title: Analysis: Distinguishing the cause of parsing failure
screens.lead: As you select each card, it flips over to reveal the cause and solution. Use the right arrow to move to the next card. Read the symptoms on the front of the card first, think about the cause, and then turn it over.

cards.front: Case 1: A descriptive sentence is added before the JSON
cards.back: This is a typical cause when only prompt instructions are written. Because there was no way to prevent the model from prepending sentences to the JSON. If you enforce the schema, the response will start straight as JSON and resolve itself.
Required fields are not specified in the schema or the schema is not enforced. Putting a field in `required` and enforcing the schema guarantees the field's existence.

cards.front: Case 3: Date value does not fit format
cards.back: This is a case where the structure is correct, but the meaning of the value is wrong. The schema only guarantees that the date is a string, but does not guarantee that it is actually a valid date. Your app must validate the value.

This is a safe denial that is independent of the schema. In OpenAI, rejection can be detected programmatically, and in Claude, if rejection occurs during streaming, `stop_reason` comes as `refusal`. It should be processed as a separate path rather than parsed.

cards.front: Case 5: JSON is truncated due to stream interruption
cards.back: An attempt was made to parse partial JSON midway or the connection was lost. It is not parsed before the stream ends, but after the block is completed.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the cause, let’s read and fix one of the poor schemas.

screens.title: Commentary: Reading and fixing poor schema
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the instructor as he steps through modifying the order extraction schema. We start with the symptoms and find the problem lines in the schema.

steps.title: Stage 1 symptoms
steps.body: In the order extraction results, `order_id` sometimes does not exist, and `total` comes as a string like `"12,000"`, breaking the total calculation. This happened even though I enforced the schema.

steps.title: Step 2 Read schema
steps.body: Reading the schema, `properties` only has `order_id`(string) and `total`(string), and there is no `required` line. A response missing `order_id` is not a schema violation because it is not required.

steps.title: Step 3 Line-by-line causes
steps.body: Because `total` is a string, a string amount is a valid value. There is no `additionalProperties`, so undefined fields may be mixed up. The symptom occurred because the scope allowed by the schema was wide, not because the enforcement did not work.

steps.title: Step 4 Modification
steps.body: Define `order_id`(string), `items`(array), and `total`(integer), put all three in `required`, and leave `additionalProperties` as false. Claude passes `output_config.format`, OpenAI passes `json_schema` and `strict: true`.

steps.title: Step 5 Remaining Work
steps.body: The app verifies that the total and item amount are correct, and that the date format is correct. If the response is rejected, it is sent to a separate path without parsing. If streaming is used together, rejection is detected as `refusal` of `stop_reason` and parsed after the stream ends.

screens.outro: Now that I've finished editing, I'll close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: formats are enforced by schemas
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Check the answer to the question posed at the beginning, namely, whether waiting can be solved by streaming and parsing failure can be solved by schema.

paragraphs: To answer your first question, both problems can be solved, but they cannot replace one another. Streaming reduces perceived latency by receiving the response in pieces, and schema ensures the structure of the output. Waiting is resolved with streaming, and parsing failure is resolved with schema.

The format is not requested by prompt, but forced by schema. Prompt instructions do not prevent missing sentences or fields, but schema enforcement ensures valid JSON, field types, and required fields. Still, the meaning of the values ​​is not guaranteed, so values ​​such as dates or sums are verified by the app.

There are some things to be careful about when using the two functions together. The JSON fragment received as a stream is not valid JSON before the end of the block, so it must be parsed after the end. Rejection responses are detected before parsing and processed separately.

In summary, apps that receive responses must be handled separately into three categories. Responses with mismatched structures are blocked by the schema, responses with mismatched values ​​are filtered out through app verification, and rejected or aborted responses are branched before parsing. If parsing failure repeats, check the log first.

callout.label: distinction to remember
callout.text: The schema is responsible for the structure, the app is responsible for the meaning of the values, and streaming is responsible for waiting.

glossary.def: The response is received incrementally as event fragments (SSE) before it is complete.
This is a blueprint that describes JSON fields, types, and whether they are required or not. Used as constraints for structured output.
This is the difference between a method that guarantees the structure through constrained decoding and a method that only asks for a sentence.
Processing that branches out before and after parsing by distinguishing between truncated responses, rejections, and value errors.

misconceptions.myth: It is enough to just write the answer in JSON.
misconceptions.fact: Prompt instructions do not prevent missing preceding or following sentences or fields. The structure must be enforced by the schema.

misconceptions.myth: If you use a schema, the values are always correct.
misconceptions.fact: A schema guarantees structure and type, but not the meaning of values. Values ​​such as dates or totals must be validated in the app.

misconceptions.myth: You can also parse JSON right away, even before the stream ends.
misconceptions.fact: The JSON fragment coming as a stream is a substring and must be parsed after the block.

misconceptions.myth: If you write down fields in the schema, they will all come in the response.
misconceptions.fact: Fields not listed as required may be omitted. Required fields must be specified as required.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The format is forced by the schema, not the prompt.
Streaming reduces perceived latency by receiving responses in pieces.
The schema guarantees the structure, and it is up to the app to verify the meaning of the values.
Rejected responses and truncated responses are detected before parsing and processed separately.

closing.reflection: What was causing JSON parsing to fail in my app?

checks.q: Instead of writing 'answer only in JSON' in the prompt, we enforced the schema. Still, what should you check directly in the app?
options: Is there an explanatory sentence in front of the JSON?
Is the date value actually a valid date?
Is the field type a string or a number?
checks.explain: Schema enforcement guarantees valid JSON, field types, and required fields, but does not guarantee the meaning of the values, so you must verify them in your app.

wrong.0: Thanks to constrained decoding, the preceding and following sentence problem is solved.
wrong.1: Required fields are guaranteed by the schema.
wrong.3: Field types are also guaranteed by the schema.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. When you select one of the views, a commentary appears. Results are not recorded.

checks.q:
I forced the schema, but order_id is sometimes missing in the response. If the schema is like below, where would I fix it first?
{"type": "object", "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}, "total": {"type": "integer"}}}
options: Add the required line to specify order_id as required.
Repeat ‘Be sure to include order_id’ three times at the prompt.
Change the type of order_id to integer.
Turn off streaming and receive responses at once
checks.explain: Even if fields that are not required are omitted, it is not a schema violation. Specifying it as required ensures that the field exists.

wrong.1: Statement repetition is not a structural guarantee, and fixing schema lines is the correct fix for the cause.
wrong.2: Changing the type does not change the existence of the field.
wrong.3: Delivery method and missing fields are two separate issues.
